q: A shelter reviews its baseline data. Which finding meets an explicit ASV indicator of a deficiency in the shelter's healthcare programme?
o: A rise in the number of animals awaiting sterilisation surgery.
An animal shows a measurable decline in physical, mental or social welfare after intake.
A disagreement between staff about the outcome of a single animal.
e: A decline in animal health and welfare after intake is a listed deficiency indicator. Waiting lists and staff disagreement reflect capacity strain or preferences, not a deficiency indicator.

q: A shelter routinely gives antibiotics to cats with sneezing and ocular discharge to prevent a viral infection from worsening. What risk does this practice create?
o: Reduced immune response to later core vaccination in those cats
False-negative results in later fungal and bacterial cultures only
Harmful side effects and the promotion of antibiotic resistance
e: Giving antibiotics when they are not indicated causes harmful side effects and promotes antibiotic resistance.

q: Which factor is one of the six that affect a shelter's capacity to provide individual medical care?
o: The likelihood of disease transmission and its consequences
The animal's breed and pedigree registration
The current adoption fee for the animal's species
e: The six factors are resources, duration of care, number needing treatment, transmission likelihood and consequences, likelihood of recovery, and live-outcome potential.

q: Under the ASV definitions, what distinguishes indirect from direct veterinary supervision?
o: The veterinarian reviews the records at least weekly and need not be reachable between those reviews.
The veterinarian must be on the premises at all times but not necessarily in the same room as the animal.
The veterinarian is off-site but has given instructions, is immediately reachable and has assumed responsibility.
e: Indirect supervision means the veterinarian need not be on the premises but has given instructions, can be reached immediately and has assumed responsibility. Direct supervision means readily available on the premises.

q: What is the ASV position on telemedicine and the veterinarian-client-patient relationship (VCPR)?
o: A VCPR can be established only through an in-person examination of every single animal in the population.
Telemedicine is acceptable for general advice but may never be used to prescribe any medication in a shelter.
Telemedicine broadens access, and the ASV supports creating VCPRs and prescribing electronically within local limits.
e: The ASV supports creating VCPRs and prescribing through telephone, digital or electronic communication, within the limits of the jurisdiction.

q: Before a medication is prescribed for a shelter animal, what does the ASV prescribing standard require?
o: A confirmatory laboratory diagnosis, a completed course of treatment and a written owner consent form
A reasonable presumptive diagnosis, the ability to administer the drug as directed and a plan to monitor the course
A veterinarian's physical examination within the previous 30 days and an approved drug formulary
e: Prescribe only with a reasonable presumptive diagnosis, the ability to administer as directed, and a plan for monitoring.

q: How does the ASV, following the World Health Organization, define health?
o: The absence of disease, infirmity and abnormal clinical signs on a full physical examination
Complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity
A state of complete physical health with no clinical or subclinical infection in any body system
e: Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

q: According to the ASV, population health is most threatened when
o: the shelter accepts more animals than can be adopted within a month, regardless of their health status.
disease spread is likely, long stays exceed the capacity for care, or one animal's costs drain resources from others.
shelter staff turn over frequently and the shelter changes its veterinary provider more than once a year.
e: Likely disease spread, over-capacity from long stays and resource-draining individual costs are the population-health threats identified by the ASV.

q: What is the purpose of a written treat-versus-cannot-treat protocol?
o: To set a maximum spending limit per animal that the veterinarian may not exceed under any circumstances
To pre-define which animals and conditions the shelter can responsibly treat, so decisions are consistent
To list the conditions that must always be referred to an outside specialty referral hospital for treatment
e: A pre-set protocol defines what the shelter can and cannot treat, supporting consistent and transparent decisions.

q: A dog has been in the shelter's foster network for 7 months. Which evaluations are overdue?
o: A quarterly reweigh and an annual comprehensive examination
A weekly weight check and a comprehensive examination every 3 months
A monthly reweigh and body condition score update, and a comprehensive examination
e: Monthly reweigh and body condition scoring are required, and a comprehensive examination is due at least every 6 months, including animals in foster care.

q: What is the maximum permissible interval between visual health observations of any individual shelter animal?
o: Every 48 hours
Every 12 hours
Every 24 hours
e: Trained personnel must visually observe every animal at least once every 24 hours.

q: When should a comprehensive physical examination ideally occur in relation to intake, and when must shelter medical care begin?
o: The examination within 72 hours of intake, with medical care beginning after the stray hold ends
The examination within 24 hours of intake, with medical care beginning at or before intake
The examination only when clinical signs appear, with medical care beginning after the first week
e: Care must begin at or before intake and continue throughout the stay. A comprehensive examination is ideally done within 24 hours, after at least a cursory assessment on arrival.

q: For which group does the ASV position statement not recommend routine FeLV and FIV testing?
o: Healthy feral cats in a trap-neuter-return programme
Cats entering group housing
Ill cats presenting with clinical signs
e: High-risk cats, including those entering group housing and those who are ill, should be tested. Testing healthy feral cats in trap-neuter-return programmes is not recommended.

q: A clinically healthy shelter cat has a single positive point-of-care FeLV test. What does the ASV recommend?
o: Do not euthanise on one positive result; confirm per AAFP guidelines and seek informed placement.
Euthanise promptly, because an FeLV-positive cat cannot be safely placed in any home or sanctuary.
Treat the result as a false positive and return the cat to general housing without any further testing.
e: The ASV does not recommend euthanising a clinically healthy cat on a single positive result. Confirmation follows AAFP guidelines, and informed placement is sought.

q: What is the ASV stance on quarantining healthy animals at intake?
o: It is not generally recommended; quarantine is reserved for animals with high-risk disease exposure.
It is required for every animal for at least 14 days, regardless of its vaccination status or signs.
It is required for all cats but not for dogs, because of the risk of feline respiratory disease.
e: Quarantining healthy animals at intake is not generally recommended, because unnecessary holds lengthen stays and harm welfare.

q: What is the ASV position when pain cannot be adequately relieved?
o: The animal should be kept as comfortable as possible until the end of the legal stray hold period.
Failure to treat pain is unacceptable, and euthanasia is a legitimate treatment when suffering cannot be relieved.
Pain that cannot be relieved should be managed with ongoing sedation until an adopter can be found.
e: Failure to treat pain is unacceptable, and treating pain can include euthanasia when suffering cannot be relieved.

q: When pain can be anticipated, such as before a surgical procedure, when should analgesia be given?
o: Immediately after the procedure, once the animal shows signs of pain
Before the painful event, at an appropriate strength and duration
At recovery, once the anaesthetic has been fully eliminated
e: The ASV recommends pre-emptive pain control before an anticipated painful event, at an appropriate strength and duration.

q: An after-hours polytrauma case cannot be stabilised, and interventions fail to relieve its distress. What is the appropriate directive?
o: Continue palliative care overnight and reassess at the start of the next shift.
Transfer the animal to another shelter without veterinary assessment.
Euthanise the animal to relieve suffering.
e: If the emergency plan cannot be implemented or fails to relieve suffering, the animal should be euthanised.

q: How does the ASV say an animal's legal status should affect its medical treatment?
o: Animals on a stray hold receive only emergency care until the hold expires.
Legal status must never interfere with necessary care of painful or significant conditions.
Treatment is provided only once the owner or the court has given written consent.
e: Legal status must never interfere with necessary preventive care or treatment of painful injuries, illness, debilitating conditions or urgent behavioural needs.

q: A shelter is legally required to hold an injured animal whose suffering cannot be alleviated. What does the ASV advise?
o: Seek permission to euthanise the animal.
Continue the legal hold with palliative care until it expires.
Release the animal to the finder for private care.
e: If suffering cannot be alleviated, the shelter should seek permission to euthanise the legally held animal.

q: What defines a disease outbreak in a shelter?
o: More than the usual number of animals affected, or an increase in the severity of cases
Three or more animals with the same clinical sign in the same week
Any confirmed case of a reportable disease in the shelter
e: An outbreak is more than the usual number of affected animals, or an increase in case severity.

q: How should an animal with suspected infectious disease be managed on arrival?
o: Isolate it until a veterinarian determines it is low risk to the population.
House it separately for 24 hours and then move it to general housing.
Keep it in general housing but with a sign on the kennel and gloves for handlers.
e: Suspected infectious animals are isolated until determined low risk. Leaving severe infectious disease in the general population is unacceptable.

q: Which is a mandatory component of a shelter's emergency medical plan under the ASV guidelines?
o: A licensed veterinarian who is physically present in the shelter every hour of every day
Care staff trained to recognise distress, injury or significant illness so prompt care or euthanasia can begin
A written agreement with a referral hospital to accept and treat every emergency case that arrives
e: The ASV requires care staff to be trained to recognise emergencies, so that timely care or humane euthanasia is not delayed.

q: A 3-week-old orphaned puppy is obtunded, hypothermic and weak. After its core temperature is stabilised, what is the highest-priority diagnostic and treatment pairing?
o: Give a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and then begin feeding.
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics and recheck temperature in 6 hours.
Check blood glucose and, if low, give diluted 50% dextrose IV or IO.
e: Neonates have minimal glycogen reserves, so blood glucose is checked and hypoglycaemia corrected with diluted dextrose. Rewarm before feeding.

q: A dyspnoeic cat has an orthopnoeic posture, open-mouth breathing and dull or absent lung sounds ventrally. What is the most likely problem and priority?
o: Pleural effusion: give oxygen and prepare for thoracocentesis.
Feline asthma: give an inhaled bronchodilator.
Upper airway obstruction: sedate and intubate.
e: Muffled or absent ventral lung sounds in a dyspnoeic cat suggest pleural effusion. Provide oxygen and prepare for thoracocentesis.

q: A hit-by-car dog has pale-to-muddy mucous membranes, a capillary refill time over 2.5 seconds and weak peripheral pulses. What state is this?
o: Decompensatory hypovolaemic shock
Compensatory hypovolaemic shock
Neurogenic shock
e: Pale or muddy membranes, prolonged refill and weak pulses indicate decompensatory hypovolaemic shock, because blood pressure can no longer be sustained.

q: A stray cat is in active generalised status epilepticus. Which sequence is the standard of care to stop the seizure?
o: An IV loading dose of phenobarbital alone, with reassessment of the seizure after 30 minutes
Oral levetiracetam followed by IM acepromazine for sedation and a quiet, dark recovery area
IV or rectal diazepam, then propofol or alfaxalone to effect if seizures persist
e: Benzodiazepines are first line to stop active seizures, followed by an injectable anaesthetic if seizures are refractory.

q: A cat with massive topical permethrin exposure has severe continuous muscle tremors. Which drug specifically addresses the tremors?
o: Atropine
Pralidoxime
Methocarbamol
e: Methocarbamol is a centrally acting muscle relaxant used to control the tremors of feline permethrin toxicosis. Atropine and pralidoxime are used for organophosphate toxicity.

q: A dog with head trauma is stuporous, with asymmetric pupils, bradycardia and rising blood pressure. Which drug is indicated for suspected raised intracranial pressure?
o: Mannitol
Dexamethasone
A rapid 90 mL/kg crystalloid bolus
e: Bradycardia with hypertension (the Cushing reflex) suggests raised intracranial pressure. Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that draws fluid out of the cerebral interstitium.

q: A shelter dog arrests during stabilisation and the ECG shows asystole. Which drug is given first in advanced life support?
o: Lidocaine
Amiodarone
Epinephrine
e: Epinephrine is the first drug for asystole, as vasoconstriction directs blood to the coronary and cerebral circulation during CPR. Lidocaine and amiodarone are antiarrhythmics for ventricular fibrillation.
